transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-05-11
Start: 14:00 PDT / 21:00 UTC
Duration: 52 mins
Attendees: Lena Carter (Redwood AE), Marco Diaz (Redwood SE), Priya Shah (Redwood CSM), Amir Patel (Peregrine Head of Platform), Sofia Nguyen (ML Eng), Ellen Brooks (InfoSec), Devon Li (SRE), Tom Harris (Product)

Summary:
High-level: scope POC acceptance criteria for latency & throughput SLOs; agree sample sizes, traffic stitching approach (mixing production-like samples with synthetic tails), and schedule for benchmark runs. Address security gating items for private pilot.

Topics:
- TTFT vs TPOT selection and hybrid SLO composition
- p95/p99 targets and risk buckets
- Warm-up/KV cache priming and measurement windows
- Traffic stitching: sampling live traffic vs synthetic heavy tails
- Measurement plan: tooling, orchestration, and artifact delivery
- Timeline and next steps for pilot kickoff

Action items (captured in metadata): see action_items field

Transcript body:
[00:00] Lena: hey everyone thanks for joining on a Monday afternoon. quick intros — i'm lena from redwood, ae. marco's our se, priya csm. over to you amir to say who you have.
[00:10] Amir: yeah thanks lena. i'm amir head of platform at peregrine. with me sofia, ellen, devon and tom. we mostly want to make sure the POC proves we can hit production latencies and not blow up cost.
[00:25] Marco: great. today's goal is to agree on acceptance criteria for latency and throughput and a repeatable measurement plan. we'll cover TTFT (time to first token) and TPOT (total per token) and propose a hybrid SLO.
[00:38] Sofia: quick note: our product needs p95 under 220ms for short prompts, p99 under 500ms for mid-length replies. those numbers are our internal desirability, not hard gating yet.
[00:50] Lena: good context. two quick clarifications: are those for user-facing interactive chat? and what's your median and tail payload size distribution?
[00:58] Sofia: mostly chat — median prompt length around 18 tokens, median response 38 tokens, but there is a long tail up to ~600 tokens for document summarization.
[01:12] Marco: ok that's helpful — the long tail matters a lot for TPOT. TTFT controls perceived latency, TPOT controls cost and capacity. we generally recommend separating them in the SLO matrix.
[01:25] Devon: how do you handle warm caches and cold starts? our traffic is bursty during business hours.
[01:33] Marco: good question — benchmark plan needs explicit warm-up phase to prime KV caches and model kernels. we do both prefix priming using a representative prompt set and also a short synthetic warm-up stream to get kernel JIT paths active.
[01:48] Ellen: for security — are you going to run benchmarks in our VPC? we need audit logs and KMS proof.
[01:55] Priya: for the pilot we can do Redwood Private (VPC) or Redwood Dedicated — both viable. we will provide SOC2 docs and KMS integration notes. i'll attach the security matrix after.
[02:05] Tom: timeline constraints: we want a pilot-ready result within three weeks, ideally sooner.
[02:11] Lena: three weeks is tight but workable if we lock scope now. our proposed schedule: week 0 - traffic sample + prompt set + security checks; week 1 - run initial TTFT baseline (hosted small runs), week 2 - larger TPOT sweep with load shaping on dedicated or private infra, week 3 - analysis and triangular acceptance. does that align?
[02:29] Amir: sounds ok. we want to keep one key success criteria — user-facing p95 <= 250ms for chat (short responses) and p99 <= 650ms overall including long tail, but we can agree on tiers.
[02:39] Marco: propose SLO matrix with buckets: short chats (<64 tokens), mid (64-256), long (>256). For each bucket measure TTFT p95/p99 and TPOT p95/p99. acceptance levels: green (meets target), amber (within 10-20%), red (misses by >20%).
[02:55] Sofia: can you give an example target numbers?
[03:00] Marco: example: short TTFT p95 180ms p99 320ms; short TPOT p95 12ms/token p99 30ms/token; mid TTFT p95 240ms p99 480ms; long TPOT is dominated by token cost — we measure overall throughput (tokens/s) per GPU and also end-to-end p99.
[03:18] Amir: our product team cares first about TTFT for chat, second about cost. so maybe weight TTFT 0.7 and TPOT 0.3 in acceptance.
[03:28] Lena: perfect, let's capture that weighting in the acceptance doc. that becomes the go/no-go rule for the pilot.
[03:35] Marco: about measurement: we will run 3 benchmark variants per bucket: 1) synthetic steady-state at median payload, 2) replay of 48h sampled traffic (stitching), 3) stress tail tests with heavy token lengths. stitching means we replay real traffic but interpolate synthetic tail events to match production burstiness.
[03:54] Devon: how do you anonymize user prompts for replay? we can't send PII.
[03:59] Lena: we'll accept customer-side anonymization — redwood provides a script that hashes identifiable fields and replaces names with placeholders; we only need token lengths and structural data to reproduce load.
[04:10] Ellen: security will need to review the anonymization script. put that on action items.
[04:15] Marco: toolchain: we use a JMeter harness for request shaping, a small runner to prime KV cache, and capture traces with per-token timestamps. results are uploaded as CSVs and a dashboard snapshot; we also attach the raw latencies and the prompt IDs (hashed).
[04:30] Tom: will you measure on our private infra or on your hosted region? differences matter for network RTT.
[04:36] Marco: yes — we'll do initial hosted runs for quick TTFT baselines, then run final acceptance tests in your VPC to remove network variance. that is part of the schedule.
[04:46] Sofia: measurement windows — how long do we run each test to get stable p99 estimates?
[04:51] Marco: p99 can be noisy. for steady-state we prefer 30 minutes of sustained load per subtest, with multiple runs (3). for stress tail tests we do ramp-up + 60 minutes of tail injection. for replay tests we can run the 48h traffic sped up but we sample to compress to 2-6 hour runs for practicality.
[05:09] Amir: what's the statistical confidence? we need to avoid fluke passes.
[05:13] Marco: we'll compute bootstrap confidence intervals for p95/p99. acceptance requires median p99 across 3 runs to be within target and 90% CI excluding red thresholds. we include full distributions in the artifact.
[05:27] Lena: also let's discuss fallback policies — if the SLOs are missed do you want auto-fallback to smaller model or more replicas?
[05:33] Tom: prefer graceful degradation — fallback to a smaller but compatible model for chat with explanatory UX. also rate limit non-critical endpoints before cutting user chat.
[05:42] Marco: Redwood supports policy-based fallback; we can demonstrate a canary that switches model family for overflow. but that will impact quality; we'll include quality regression checks in the playbook.
[05:52] Sofia: does quantization affect TTFT? we worry about hallucination regressions.
[05:56] Marco: quantization usually reduces TPOT significantly and slightly improves TTFT; regression risk depends on model and task. we'll run an A/B between FP16 and a quantized variant and include an eval suite for quality checks.
[06:08] Ellen: about audit logs — we need proof of request/response lineage and KMS envelope logs for key operations.
[06:15] Priya: we'll provide the audit schema in the security pack and confirm KMS calls are recorded. there's a template.
[06:20] Amir: great. i want to agree success criteria now in the call: pilot success = (1) TTFT weighted score >= 0.7 pass, (2) cost within 20% of forecast for target throughput, (3) no open critical security findings. is that acceptable?
[06:35] Lena: yes let's put that in the SLO charter: scoring function with TTFT weight 0.7, TPOT weight 0.3, cost multiplier, and security gating.
[06:44] Tom: do we commit to a single dedicated machine spec for TPOT tests? we need to size for our concurrency -- expected concurrent sessions 450 peak.
[06:53] Marco: for sizing we'll propose two configs: worker A (8xA100-style equiv) and worker B (4xH100 equiv) depending on availability; we'll run capacity sweeps to find tokens/s per worker and recommend commit.
[07:05] Devon: concurrency pattern: 450 concurrent chat sessions, average think time 7s, bursts up to 1200 sustained for 2-5 minutes.
[07:15] Marco: that burst info helps with autoscale policy tests — we'll simulate ramp and observe queueing.
[07:20] Sofia: instrumentations: we need per-token timing and prefix cache hit rates.
[07:25] Marco: yes we capture KV cache hit rates, batching stats, queue latency, and first-token micro-timings. these are included in the artifact CSV.
[07:34] Amir: about traffic stitching — can you expand the method? i'm trying to picture how the 48h sample becomes a 3-hour run.
[07:42] Marco: sure. we compress time by preserving relative inter-arrival patterns per user session and we maintain the burst correlation. we keep the same session sequences but speed them up, then we overlay synthetic long-tail tasks where real logs lack examples, to ensure the model experiences the long tail. it's not perfect but gives representative stress.
[07:58] Ellen: will the compressed replay distort caches?
[08:02] Marco: we account for that. we run a longer warm-up with the sampled prefixes before the actual measurement window to prime caches proportionally. and we record prefix reuse stats to show the effect of compression.
[08:14] Tom: what's your suggested TTFT target to propose to execs? we're conservative.
[08:18] Lena: given your median sizes, we propose short TTFT p95 200ms, p99 380ms; mid TTFT p95 320ms p99 520ms. present these as proposal, open to negotiation.
[08:30] Amir: ok let's tentatively accept those as targets for pilot gating.
[08:33] Sofia: how do we capture noise from network variability?
[08:36] Marco: run final acceptance in your VPC where network is stable; also use synthetic RTT injection to emulate cross-region users for separate tests.
[08:45] Priya: i'll put together the acceptance matrix doc and post to shared drive, include weighting formula and CSV schema.
[08:51] Lena: now timeline specifics: amir will deliver traffic sample by Fri (2027-05-14). Marco will produce runbook by Thu 2027-05-13. we aim for initial hosted TTFT baseline Tues 2027-05-18 18:00 UTC. final VPC acceptance scheduled for week of 2027-05-24.
[09:06] Amir: yes that works.
[09:09] Ellen: security question — if we use Redwood Dedicated, does data ever traverse external regions? need to confirm data residency.
[09:18] Priya: Dedicated can be pinned to a region, and with Private we can deploy into your VPC; we'll include residency commitments in the SO.
[09:26] Sofia: what about monitoring during pilot? can we get the console dashboards?
[09:30] Marco: yes we'll grant read-only dashboard access for the pilot, including per-route token cost and time-series for p95/p99.
[09:36] Tom: will you provide a benchmark summary template?
[09:39] Marco: yes, a skeleton report with graphs, recommended commit sizing, and CI artifacts.
[09:44] Lena: ok any final questions?
[09:46] Devon: how do we handle model fallbacks and quality checks in the runbook?
[09:49] Marco: we include a rollback/fallback run: the A/B compares primary vs fallback model for 30 minutes, and we run a small automated eval set (50 prompts) to detect quality delta exceeding agreed threshold.
[09:59] Sofia: can you include the eval prompts? we'll provide a gold set of 200 prompts for quality checks.
[10:04] Marco: perfect, we'll run the eval before and after quantization or fallback.
[10:08] Lena: to close, i'll email the pilot charter and acceptance matrix by EOD tomorrow. we'll link the runbook and benchmark harness.
[10:16] Amir: thanks everyone, excited to get started.
[10:19] Lena: thanks all.
